questions.question: In a FIFO queue, offer(e) adds and poll() removes. Which element does poll() return?
options: The most recently added element
The earliest added element still present
The smallest element by natural ordering
A randomly chosen element
questions.explanation: FIFO means first-in, first-out: poll() always removes from the head, which is the oldest element still in the queue.

questions.question: Which java.util.Queue method returns null on an empty queue instead of throwing?
options: remove()
element()
poll()
getFirst()
questions.explanation: poll() and peek() are the tolerant forms that return null when empty; remove(), element() and getFirst() throw NoSuchElementException.

questions.question: Queue<String> q is empty. What does q.element() do?
options: Returns null
Returns an empty Optional
Blocks until an element arrives
Throws NoSuchElementException
questions.explanation: element() is the throwing twin of peek(): it inspects the head and throws NoSuchElementException when the queue is empty.

questions.question: A capacity-restricted queue is full. How does add(e) differ from offer(e)?
options: add throws IllegalStateException; offer returns false
add returns false; offer throws IllegalStateException
Both return false without inserting
Both throw IllegalStateException
questions.explanation: The Queue contract pairs add/offer: add signals failure with IllegalStateException, offer signals it by returning false.

questions.question: Why does ArrayDeque reject null elements with a NullPointerException?
options: Arrays cannot store null references
The Deque interface bans null in every implementation
null is the sentinel that peek/poll use to mean 'empty'
null would corrupt the backing array's hashCode
questions.explanation: peek() and poll() return null to mean 'no element', so storing a real null would make emptiness undetectable. LinkedList, by contrast, does permit nulls.

questions.question: Which ArrayDeque method pair gives LIFO stack behaviour?
options: offer and poll
addLast and pollFirst
add and remove
push and pop
questions.explanation: push/pop are aliases for addFirst/removeFirst, so both ends of the operation hit the head, producing LIFO order.

questions.question: A PriorityQueue<Integer> using natural ordering holds 7, 2 and 9. What does peek() return?
options: 7, the first element inserted
2, the smallest element
9, the largest element
null until the queue is sorted
questions.explanation: A PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default, so its head is the least element according to the ordering, returned by peek() in O(1).

questions.question: Which structure produces a level-order (breadth-first) traversal of a binary tree?
options: A stack
A priority queue keyed by node depth
A FIFO queue
Plain recursion with no auxiliary structure
questions.explanation: BFS enqueues children as it dequeues parents, so nodes come out in the order they were discovered, which is level by level.

questions.question: With head = 6 and size = 4 in this 8-slot ring buffer, which index does the next enqueue write to?
questions.explanation: The tail index is (head + size) % capacity, so (6 + 4) % 8 = 2, wrapping around past the end of the array.

questions.question: A ring buffer stores only head and tail. head == tail is ambiguous. Which fix distinguishes full from empty?
options: Make the capacity a power of two
Test whether (tail - head + n) % n equals zero
Initialise tail to -1 instead of 0
Keep an explicit count, or always leave one slot unused
questions.explanation: Only extra information breaks the tie: a size counter, or sacrificing one slot so full means (tail + 1) % n == head. Modular arithmetic alone cannot tell the two states apart.

questions.question: Comparing ArrayDeque and LinkedList used purely as a FIFO Queue, which claim is correct?
options: LinkedList wins: it never has to copy an array
ArrayDeque wins: no per-element nodes, better locality
Only LinkedList implements the Queue interface
ArrayDeque cannot grow beyond its initial capacity
questions.explanation: ArrayDeque stores elements in a circular array with no node objects, so it allocates less and is cache-friendlier; both offer amortized O(1) enqueue and dequeue.

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?

Both calls throw NullPointerException
true is printed, then the ArrayDeque offer throws NPE
Both calls return false and nothing is inserted
questions.explanation: LinkedList permits null elements, so its offer returns true; ArrayDeque forbids null and throws NullPointerException immediately.

questions.question: Which statement about java.util.PriorityQueue is true?
options: Its iterator returns elements in sorted order
It is thread-safe for multiple producer threads
poll() is O(1) because the head is cached
offer and poll are O(log n); peek is O(1)
questions.explanation: A binary heap sifts along one root-to-leaf path for offer and poll, giving O(log n), while peek just reads slot 0. PriorityQueue is unsynchronized and its iteration order is unspecified.

questions.question: A consumer thread calls take() on an empty LinkedBlockingQueue. What happens?
options: It returns null immediately
It throws NoSuchElementException
It blocks until an element arrives or the thread is interrupted
It spins and returns false after a default timeout
questions.explanation: take() and put() are the blocking pair of BlockingQueue: take() parks the caller until an element is available, throwing InterruptedException if interrupted.

questions.question: Which statement about ArrayBlockingQueue and LinkedBlockingQueue is correct?
options: Both are unbounded unless externally wrapped
Both require an explicit capacity argument
ArrayBlockingQueue grows; LinkedBlockingQueue is fixed
ArrayBlockingQueue: fixed capacity; LinkedBlockingQueue: optional
questions.explanation: ArrayBlockingQueue must be given a capacity at construction and never grows; LinkedBlockingQueue accepts an optional bound and otherwise caps at Integer.MAX_VALUE.

questions.question: In this BFS, why is the queue size captured into sz before the inner loop?
options: To avoid a ConcurrentModificationException
So each outer iteration processes exactly one level
Because size() is O(n) on ArrayDeque
To stop the backing array from resizing mid-traversal
questions.explanation: The snapshot freezes how many nodes belong to the current level, so children added during the inner loop are handled by the next outer iteration.

questions.question: A queue is built from two stacks, in and out, moving elements only when out is empty. What is the cost of dequeue?
options: O(1) worst case for every dequeue
O(n) for every dequeue
Amortized O(1), though one dequeue can cost O(n)
O(log n) amortized
questions.explanation: Each element is pushed and popped at most twice overall, so n operations cost O(n) total, but the single dequeue that triggers a transfer is O(n).

questions.question: A linked queue keeps head and tail pointers. When dequeue removes the last remaining node, what else must happen?
options: head must be reassigned to tail
tail must also be set to null
tail must keep pointing at the removed node
Nothing; tail is recomputed on the next enqueue
questions.explanation: If tail still references the detached node, the next enqueue links onto an unreachable node, so the element is lost and the old node leaks.

questions.question: For a PriorityQueue holding n elements, what is the cost of remove(someValue) for an arbitrary value?
options: O(n): it scans for the element, then sifts
O(log n): the heap locates it by comparisons
O(1): the heap indexes elements by value
O(n log n): the whole heap is rebuilt
questions.explanation: remove(Object) does a linear indexOf scan over the backing array, then an O(log n) sift, so the scan dominates at O(n) - unlike poll(), which is O(log n).

questions.question: Which statement about ConcurrentLinkedQueue is accurate?
options: size() traverses the nodes, so it is O(n)
take() blocks until an element becomes available
It is bounded and rejects offers when full
Its iterator throws ConcurrentModificationException
questions.explanation: ConcurrentLinkedQueue keeps no element counter, so size() walks the list and may be inexact under concurrency. It is unbounded, non-blocking, and its iterator is weakly consistent.
